newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Marcos decree bails out 21 jailed Chinese.
newsitem.headline: Marcos decree bails out 21 jailed Chinese.

text.p: A Philippine judge, citing a martial law decree by the late dictator Ferdinand Marcos, on Wednesday dismissed charges of illegal entry against 21 Chinese fishermen arrested in waters claimed by Manila and Beijing.

Judge Eliodoro Ubiadas ordered the release of the fishermen, who have been detained by police in Subic town, 80 km (50 miles) northwest of Manila, since the Philippine Navy arrested them on May 20 off Scarborough Shoal in the South China Sea.
Ubiadas told Reuters he threw out the case because the charges were "prematurely filed" as it had not been established that the disputed shoal was within Philippine territory.

He said he based his ruling on a decree issued by Marcos in the late 1970s that defines Philippine territorial boundaries and provides that overlapping claims over a territory within this country's special economic zone -- set at 200 nautical miles from the shore -- must be resolved by an agreement among claimants.

Ownership of Scarborough Shoal has not been determined by any agreement between Manila and Beijing and "so my conclusion is the filing of illegal entry charges is premature", the judge said by telephone.
Marcos was ousted after 20 years in power by a popular revolt in 1986, but a number of the decrees he issued with his martial law powers remain in force. He died in exile in Hawaii in 1989.
The Chinese embassy in Manila has demanded the release of the fishermen, saying they were in Chinese territory when the Philippine Navy apprehended them and impounded their boat.
Beijing says all the isles, reefs and shoals in the South China Sea historically belong to China. Manila says the shoal is within its exclusive economic zone and it has sole sovereignty over it.
The shoal lies well north of the Spratly islands, a cluster of potentially oil-rich isles, shoals and atolls that Beijing says has also been Chinese territory since ancient times.
The Spratlys are also claimed wholly or in part by Vietnam, Taiwan, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei.
Ubiadas said state prosecutors had informed him they were preparing separate charges of illegal fishing against the Chinese, but the prosecutors were unable to produce the fish.

The arrest of the fishermen, who were expected to be released from prison in the next few days, was part of a series of incidents involving Chinese and Filipinos in the disputed South China Sea that has strained relations between Manila and Beijing.

The Philippines in May protested against alleged trespassing by Chinese naval ships in an area it claims in the Spratlys. China, in turn, accused Manila of violating Chinese sovereignty after a group of Filipino fishermen raised their country's flag over Scarborough Shoal.
